definition.text: A family of results showing that repeated games have a great many equilibrium outcomes: almost any payoff can be sustained if players are patient enough.

facts.text: It got its name because game theorists widely knew the result in the 1950s although nobody had published it.
'Almost any' means every payoff that is feasible and individually rational, that is, better than what each player can guarantee alone.
The simplest proof uses a grim trigger strategy: cooperate until someone deviates, then punish them forever.
Friedman's 1971 version strengthened it to subgame-perfect equilibria, where punishment threats must be credible.
It explains why agreements between countries are kept without enforcement: relations are long-term, though an impatient country is hard to punish credibly.
In a close-knit community it shows how traditions and taboos can be upheld by social norms.
Franklin Fisher noted it is not a positive theory: it does not predict what firms will do, only that cost and demand alone cannot explain oligopoly.

definition.text: A situation in a game where no player could do better by changing only their own strategy while everyone else keeps theirs.

facts.text: It is used to analyse any strategic interaction, where each decision-maker's outcome depends on the others' choices as well as their own.
Nash's insight was that the choices of several decision-makers cannot be predicted by analysing each one in isolation.
It is named after John Forbes Nash Jr., but Antoine Augustin Cournot used the same idea in 1838 for firms choosing how much to produce.
A Nash equilibrium need not be Pareto optimal, so it can look irrational from outside: everyone could be better off.
In sequential games it can rest on threats players would never carry out; subgame perfect equilibrium removes these.
It is applied to predict traffic flows, where each traveller's route time depends on the routes everyone else picks.
John Maynard Smith applied the concept to model the evolution of behaviour in 1982.

definition.text: A Nash equilibrium in which at least one player randomizes, choosing among strategies with set probabilities rather than always playing the same one.

facts.text: In the drive-on-the-left-or-right game, besides the two pure equilibria there is a third where each side is chosen with 50% probability.
In matching pennies, where one player wins on a match and the other on a mismatch, the only equilibrium is mixed.
An equilibrium is strict if every player would lose by switching, and weak if some player is indifferent.

definition.text: A refinement of Nash equilibrium that is stable against deviations by any coalition of players, not just by single players.

facts.text: Ordinary Nash equilibrium counts only individual deviations, which is not convincing enough for cooperative games.

definition.text: Nash's theorem that every game with finitely many players and finitely many pure strategies has at least one Nash equilibrium once mixed strategies are allowed.

facts.text: Equilibria may fail to exist when choices are infinite and unbounded, as when two players name numbers and the larger wins.
Nash's thesis proof used Brouwer's fixed-point theorem; his 1950 paper used the simpler Kakutani fixed-point theorem.
Robert Wilson's 1971 oddness theorem says almost all finite games have a finite, odd number of Nash equilibria.
